subsubtopic: ARRANGEMENTS FOR BRITISH COLUMBIA COASTAL TRAFFIC
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. Yesterday members of parliament of all parties from British Columbia received information that the joint agreement between Coast Ferries Limited and Rivtow Straits Limited has now broken up. Can the minister advise what arrangement he or the government have made to ensure that the coast traffic, which the minister's action of some months ago seemed to jeopardize to an incredible degree, will finally be put back on a proper basis for the citizens of the coastal ports of British Columbia?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: ARRANGEMENTS FOR BRITISH COLUMBIA COASTAL TRAFFIC
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have not yet had a chance to focus on that statement of fact with regard to the relationship of these two companies. I should say to the hon. member that the greater part of the involvement of Coast Ferries was in an area of service which has never had a subsidy. That was one the critical questions facing us as a matter of policy, the extent to which subsidized and non-subsidized ferries could be operating side by side.

subsubtopic: ARRANGEMENTS FOR BRITISH COLUMBIA COASTAL TRAFFIC
speechtext: Every one who has looked into this issue on the west coast has agreed that the service was effective until the minister meddled and that it is now non-effective. Has the minister received any official word or taken cognizance of any official word that this joint enterprise has broken up? Does the minister have a statement to make to the people of British Columbia who are dependent upon that service which is now in jeopardy?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: ARRANGEMENTS FOR BRITISH COLUMBIA COASTAL TRAFFIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I said in my first answer, the service in which Coast Ferries was involved was essentially a non-subsidized service. That, of course, was a problem that we foresaw. Of course, there will always be difficulties in the transport of goods by water and to remote areas and the challenges of trying to do it effectively. The point that we were trying to accomplish was better total transportation facilities for that area over a period of time by ceasing to expend large amounts of money on annual subsidies for particular types of movement in the face of development of some alternatives which are probably cost effective. That means they can produce far better transportation for those people involved over a period of time if we spend on such things as airports, navigational aids and the like.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR DETAILS OF BID BY CROWN CORPORATIONS ON PROJECT IN VENEZUELA
speechtext: I do know there is a Canadian consortium which is interested in bidding on this multimillion dollar project in Venezuela. I believe the deadlines are some time around December 6. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 should also like to direct a question to the Prime Minister with reference to his request to the former President of the Treasury Board some three and a half years ago to investigate what the Prime Minister regarded as an extremely serious and potentially embarrassing situation. Does the Prime Minister regard the course of action taken by the President of the Treasury Board at that time, namely, making only one telephone call to an important official of the company, but not having consulted at all with the former Auditor General who drew the matter to the Prime Minister's attention in the first place, as being sufficient action over the three and a half year period of time to constitute an adequate investigation into this matter?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: SUFFICIENCY OF ACTION TO INVESTIGATE PAYMENT OF REBATES INTO SWISS BANK ACCOUNTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there seems to be some argumentative aspect to this question which I have answered in the past several days several times. May I repeat that the test should not be whether one telephone call or 50 were necessary. The test should be whether the telephone call produced the intended result, and from all the evidence we have it did. The telephone call brought forth the evidence that the subject had been raised by the former Auditor General who, let us not forget, signed the audited books and the report of Polymer; the matter had been discussed with Mr. Hampson, President of the DC, the disagreement between Mr. Hampson and the auditors, Peat, Marwick and Mitchell, and he challenged Mr. Henderson to disagree if he thought there was something untoward. Not only was there no disagreement, Mr. Henderson signed the audited books and the auditor's report for that particular year, and the leader of the NDP can see that. Having obtained those results from one phone call, I do not see why the hon. member argues that perhaps 50 phone calls would have been better.

speechtext:

subtopic: CROWN CORPORATIONS' BID ON VENEZUELAN PROJECT-PRIME MINISTER'S KNOWLEDGE OF USE OF AGENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is supplementary to those asked by my colleagues from Vegreville and Central Nova and relates to the Canaven negotiation in which the Prime Minister himself in September, as my colleague from Vegreville indicated, became involved by personally promising more federal financial backing in this matter. Given the prevailing interest in agency arrangements involving Crown corporations and the possible effect upon Canada's international reputation of this kind of arrangement, will the Prime Minister tell the House whether he has sought and received a full briefing on all the agent arrangements and other aspects of the Canaven negotiations.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: CROWN CORPORATIONS' BID ON VENEZUELAN PROJECT-PRIME MINISTER'S KNOWLEDGE OF USE OF AGENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I indicated in answer to an earlier question, this matter was discussed between other ministers and myself several weeks ago. It was at that time I believe 1 was reminded of the deadline of early December. The question at that time was the extent of the exposure of the Canadian government in any unsuccessful conclusion of the operation.
Certainly what I said in September still stands; that is, we want to encourage this project and even involve ourselves in some risk as it concerns the question of viable economic fall-out for Canada and I believe this procedure is reciprocated by the Venezuelan government which would be interested in seeing Canada get the contract. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE SERIOUSLY RECOMMENDATIONS OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
That this House condemns the government for its failure to take seriously the recommendations made year after year by the Auditor General, and calls on the government (a) to take steps to ensure that the annual financial reports of all Crown corporations are referred to the appropriate committees of the House of Commons;
(ft) to provide the Standing Committee on Public Accounts with adequate staff so that it can do its job thoroughly; and
(c) to appoint immediately a comptroller general as recommended in the Auditor General's report for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1976.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Canadians have witnessed for more than a decade the spectacle of auditors general in sequence publishing ever lengthening lists and detailed reports of mismanagement by this government on the one hand and, on the other, the government responsible for this waste failing year after year to take the slightest bit of corrective action. The Liberal cabinet has ignored the Auditor General and ignored what have properly become known as "horror stories". I will not waste time this afternoon listing all the examples of mismanagement with which we have become all too familiar in this House. The worst examples have already become part of Canadian folk lore-acres of unused office space, fishing boats
Auditor General
which will not float, boots for one foot only, and so on. Neither Farley Mowat nor our fine Canadian poet, Earl Birney, could have known that their delightful fiction would be produced, live and in living incompetence, not by the National Film Board but by the Liberal cabinet and a host of senior bureaucrats in Ottawa.
The humour associated with such mismanagement, if ever there was any, has long since gone. The demands of those of us in opposition over the years have now been joined by almost every taxpayer in the country. Knowledge of this government's incompetence has escaped no one. Excuse me, Mr. Speaker; it has escaped a few: the Liberal cabinet alone remains deaf to the universal demand for corrective action. As members of parliament, neither we nor the cabinet can ignore the Auditor General when he says:
I am deeply concerned that, on the evidence of the two-year examination carried out by the audit office, parliament-and indeed the governement-has lost or is close to losing effective control of the public purse.
That is a serious judgment made by a serious man. As I said, we cannot ignore this carefully-considered statement and the damning evidence contained in the report which substantiates it.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), unfortunately, has ignored the documented mismanagement of the government year after year. He has never shown concern about financial control. Indeed, as events of recent days make abundantly clear, he wants now to ignore and hide the mismanagement of the nation's Crown corporations. Despite 3 'A years of knowledge of financial shiftiness, to put it politely, by Polysar Limited, knowledge provided by the former auditor general about activities which might well include criminal offences either at home or abroad, the Prime Minister is still unprepared to take corrective steps to end the objectionable behavior. Witness the supercilious attitude which the Prime Minister made evident not more than 45 minutes ago in the House when he answered questions asked by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), myself and other members of opposition parties. He simply does not care.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE SERIOUSLY RECOMMENDATIONS OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext: Right.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE SERIOUSLY RECOMMENDATIONS OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Instead of attacking the problem, the Prime Minister responded facetiously to criticisms of Crown corporations by attacking the Crown corporations and saying that maybe they should be turned over to private control. He deals with such serious questions by trying to brush them off with flippant comments. Crown corporations in our country ought to be efficient, they ought to be honest and free of meddling. Crown corporations, as we well know in this House, have been operated at arm's length so they can be free of political meddling in their day to day operations. But what has happened after the years of control exercised by the Liberal government over our Crown corporations? Listen to what the Auditor General has to say in his report-and I say to cabinet ministers who are present this afternoon, read the report with care if you have not done so already.
1562

Auditor General
Talking about our once glorious Crown corporations, our Auditor General says, first, that no central government agency recognizes the need to identify all corporations owned or controlled by the government of Canada. Second, commercial enterprises in the private sector are subject to a greater degree of financial accountability than Crown corporations. Third, financial management and control is not a priority within Crown corporations. Fourth, the annual deficits and net debt of the government of Canada are substantially understated due to the manner of accounting for Crown corporations. Fifth, parliament is presented with incomplete and fragmented financial plans and inadequate financial reports. Sixth, financing practices would preclude evaluating management performance even if central agencies had the responsibility to do so. As a result of these observations and other findings, the Auditor General reached a very serious and sad conclusion, and I quote:
In the majority of the Crown corporations audited by the Auditor General, financial management and control is weak and ineffective. Moreover, co-ordination and guidance by central government agencies of financial management and control practices in these Crown corporations are virtually non-existent.
What a shattering indictment of the Liberal government. What a complete summary of mishandling of what should be the proudest set of corporations in our land, those directly responsible to a nationally elected government. The Liberals have erroneously translated an arm's length relationship to mean financial indifference. The result has been utter financial chaos. It is as serious as that.

speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby has the floor for the purpose of making a speech. I suggest that we listen.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE SERIOUSLY RECOMMENDATIONS OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
It has been correctly pointed out that when a Liberal makes an interjection, it ought to be both factual and intelligent. He is normally neither. The principle of an arm's length relationship with Crown corporations is valid for most aspects of their existence but, emphatically, that does not mean that Crown corporations should be free of scrutiny of their financial operations by parliament or that their standards of business ethics can be a matter of total indifference to the government.
Neither financial incompetence nor moral turpitude is tolerable to the people of Canada. They are, after all, the shareholders of Crown corporations. They want their money spent intelligently and honestly. At the end of each year the financial operations of Crown corporations must be open to exami-

nation by parliament. If at any time morally unsound actions are discovered, they must be stopped.
As it states in the motion now before the House, financial reports of every Crown corporation in Canada should automatically be sent to the appropriate committee of the House of Commons for examination. It is in this sense that we believe Crown corporations must be accountable to parliament. To make this possible, the committees, and the public accounts committee in particular, must have the staff to do an adequate job of examining these reports and other matters. As every member of this House knows, at present the staffing requirements are so inadequately filled that members cannot do the minimum job expected of them in terms of assessing the financial operations of this government.
I wish to say something in general about the central recommendation in the Auditor General's report, namely, the recommendation that we establish in Canada a comptroller general as a general supervisor of government spending. This key recommendation was made after a comprehensive two-year study. It was not lightly made nor was it casually thrown out. The Auditor General's discoveries are deeply disturbing. He found an indifferent attitude among senior government managers. It was not their money with which they dealt; therefore, they simply did not care. In his judgment there was an utter lack of comprehension of what financial control really means. Among the senior civil servants there was a total absence of knowledge of what senior management roles are when it comes to enduring financial control. The Auditor General attempted to explain why this situation has been allowed to develop. He said that despite an expansion of the Treasury Board staff, Treasury Board simply cannot cope with the problems because it is overburdened with other responsibilities, including the recently acquired responsibility for collective bargaining and implementing the Official Languages Act.
The Auditor General called for four sensible basic requirements for the federal government to achieve effective financial management and control-four basic requirements that had been systematically ignored by the government. The first is a financial plan that serves as a cornerstone for managing and controlling financial resources. Second is a central system of budgetary control based on an effectively functioning control system in each department and agency. That is crucial. Third, complete and appropriate financial reports. Fourth, effective financial control based on a system of continuous and automatic check on expenditure decisions. It is a lamentable fact, but a fact, nonetheless, that he should have to recommend that these steps be taken when year after year his predecessor documented evidence of grotesque mismanagement. We should not now, in 1976, be calling for these sensible proposals to be implemented: they should have been implemented years ago. To achieve these objectives, the Auditor General also recommended, and I quote:
The establishment of the position of chief financial officer of the government, preferably with the title comptroller general of Canada, with deputy minister status and a direct reporting relationship to the President of the Treasury Board,
December 1, 1976

and with duties and authorities fully commensurate with the important responsibilities of such a key position-
In the time left to me, I wish to deal with the pitiful excuses of the Prime Minister for failing to implement this central recommendation of the Auditor General. They are excuses which I believe are based on deliberately misleading and erroneous information provided by senior bureaucrats, I suspect, in a highly self-serving way. This does not, of course, lessen the Prime Minister's responsibility but only indicates that the government and parliament not only have lost control of the purse but have failed to maintain their over-all ascendancy over the senior civil servants: either that, or the Prime Minister had deliberately passed on erroneous information to members of the House of Commons and to the people of Canada. What did the Prime Minister actually say? I quote from his press conference of just a few days ago. Referring to the Auditor General, the Prime Minister said:
He said the way to control it from the top is to name a comptroller general, not the kind of one we had before the Glassco commission but a new one. If I understand him correctly, he calls him an umpire.
We don't quite understand and I don't think he, himself, is quite sure as to what the umpiring would be between, what parties. In other words, how do you exercise the responsibility? Is the umpiring between the ministers and their deputies, or is the umpiring between the deputies and the Treasury Board, or is the umpiring between the deputies and myself? Because they are responsible to me in the very real sense.
There we have the Prime Minister at his Jesuitical best, trying to totally confuse the issue by asking a series of unrelated questions. This is the red herring which the Prime Minister has introduced to justify a totally unnecessary royal commission. This is the escapist argument he uses to cover up his government's failure to end financial mismanagement by implementing a sensible recommendation to appoint a comptroller general.
The Auditor General has openly and honestly explained that the reference to an umpire which he made many months ago was confusing, and at that time he went to the Treasury Board and explained precisely what he meant by the term. So there is no excuse now for present members of the Treasury Board who are passing on advice to the Prime Minister to remain in a state of confusion. They have known for months precisely what the Auditor General had in mind, and if there is any doubt remaining, his recent report spells it out clearly. It is well within the limits of established parliamentary procedures followed in Canada and elsewhere. In the course of a recent television program, the Auditor General had this to say:
I haven't recommended anything that has any constitutional implications at all, as far as I can see. If I can boil this down in a nutshell, the government now has, in round numbers, say, 30 deputy ministers. What I have said is that one of those deputy ministers, and a pretty senior deputy minister, namely, the secretary of the Treasury Board, has a very large conglomeration of duties attaching to his position over and above financial management control, which is one of them. He has six deputies reporting to him. Financial control of public funds is such an important function that I have, in effect, said: Let us have two deputy ministers reporting to the President of the Treasury Board.
It is as simple as that. I would have thought that even a Liberal cabinet could have comprehended it. He wants the
Auditor General
cabinet to recognize the clear truth that the present deputy minister of the Treasury Board has too much to do, and since financial control is of such major importance, its function should be separated and made the exclusive responsibility of one deputy minister.
Allan Lambert, a favourite of the government, recently-appointed chairman of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Financial Organization and Accountability, which is central to the issue under discussion here, has given his support to the Auditor General. Far from criticizing the recommendation that a comptroller be appointed, he sees it as essentially complementing his work. Here is what Mr. Lambert has said:
The royal commission would not be affronted nor its work hampered in any way if any and all of the Auditor General's recommendations, including that for a comptroller general, were implemented immediately.
Mr. Lambert added that he has already informed the government, presumably either the Prime Minister or the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras), of his views on the matter. So here we have a case where the chairman of a royal commission set up to deal with the broader aspects of the subject joins the Auditor General in recommending the establishment of the position of comptroller general. Both reject the government's refusal to do so, precisely because they recognize the phony arguments of the government for what they are.
Finally, the government and its ministers must change their extravagant ways. A good part of political life is unconnected with law-making or debates in the House of Commons. A great deal of importance attaches to the style of existence of politicians themselves. The Prime Minister, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), to name a few members of the cabinet, have failed to set a good example. In fact, their example of waste, of extravagance and of lack of concern about taxpayers' money has done just the opposite. The Prime Minister has spent so much money on his official residence since he came to office that he has so far refused to answer questions on the subject which have been on the order paper for months. He refuses to answer because, according to some official in the government, embarrassment would be the result.
The Minister of Transport, dear old Otto, has logged more flying hours, I am sure, than any of the pilots employed by his department. It is our view that what might be described as the maximization of conspicuous consumption on the part of cabinet ministers should come to an end. It is time another style of life was followed in the conduct of their offices. Cabinet ministers should set an example of restraint; they should set a standard, not of consumption but of decency. That is what the people expect, but it is not what they are getting. I regret to add that senior civil servants in too many cases have taken this bad example coming from the cabinet and have made it the basis of their own operations.
The attitude which the Auditor General has documented in his report seems increasingly to be: Who cares? Well, the people who pay the bills care, and they are now piping a new tune. That tune is: The Jig is Up. They want government programs; there is no question about that. They want govern-

It indicates a mentality which I want to elaborate on in my remarks because the real issue here is not just whether this government ignores the urgings of the Auditor General; the real issue is that this is a government which consistently ignores the whole subject of its financial management and its financial accountability. It is not only that the Auditor General expresses-and I point out to the House what the Auditor General pointed out in words which he chose with particular care-his concern that this government's spending is virtually out of control; the central point is that this government has consistently shown no interest whatsoever in improving either the efficiency or the standards by which it conducts the nation's affairs. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE SERIOUSLY RECOMMENDATIONS OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
The backbenchers of the party opposite make clear by their words and interjections what ministers of the government have made clear in their conduct, which is that principles of openness, principles affecting rules of conduct, standards to guide governments for the reassertion of the role and responsibilities of parliament, are principles alien to the Liberal approach to government in Canada. Unfortunately, sir, we are left to draw public attention to the worst excesses of this administration and lend our support to true public servants like the Auditor General who seek to promote constructive and necessary change. It is in that context that I have no difficulty, and a great deal of enthusiasm, in supporting the essence of the motion before this House.
80005-32i/2

December 1, 1976
Auditor General
[ Translation]
Mr. Charles-Eug&ne Dionne (Kamouraska): Mr. Speaker, the subject of the matter being debated today sums up the concern of Canadians which has surfaced since the Auditor General of Canada published his report for the fiscal year ended on March 31, 1976. It is not the first time recommendations are being made by those whose responsibility is to audit the often extravagant expenditures made by some departments.
In such a situation, it is fitting that the government take seriously the Auditor General's recommendations to appoint a comptroller general and take steps to ensure that the annual financial reports of all Crown corporations be referred to the appropriate committees of the House of Commons. It is obvious that accounting errors have been repeatedly pointed out. It is not for nothing that the Glassco Commission was set up some years ago; its report did show that expenditures had been exaggerated in several areas. Since then, the following governments have not made any great effort to improve the situation.
I understand that supervision and control of expenditures is not an easy task. However, when practical suggestions are drawn to the attention of the government by those who are responsible for auditing the accounts, it is normal that decisions should be taken by the authorities. We can read some comments which could create much concern among the people one of which is a report in a Montreal newspaper headlined "Ottawa has lost all effective control over public funds" and I quote a few excerpts of that report:
The government, and consequently Parliament itself, has gradually lost all control o''er public funds and has taken no concrete action to correct the weaknesses of the present treasury control and management system, which is judged "ineffective". The Secretariat of the Treasury Board should be completely reorganized and the management of public funds should be handed over to a general financial comptroller who would have the position of deputy minister.
One of the main causes of the bad financial management of the government is the lack of real and general understanding among senior government officials of what constitutes effective management and control of public funds.
This article also states, and I quote:
The report reveals the fact that the government does not have an exhaustive list of all associations, agencies and corporations in which it has interests, and that consequently the government cannot have any effective control over the management of the public funds for which it is responsible. This year, the study dealt mostly with the management systems of Crown corporations rather than of departments. Present directives and policies concerning the allocation and distribution of government offices show that certain present practices have a tendency to promote inefficient space utilisation and give the impression of overly expensive planning. As concerns travel expenses, the departments, reviewed make no real effort to ensure that the directives are implemented.
The Canadian International Development Agency (CIDA) spent approximately $826,000 on March 31, 1976, to purchase and outfit a fishing vessel which was afterwards discovered to be unfit for sailing. Because of transportation delays and insufficient protection of the shipment, potatoes sent to Haiti by CIDA were completely rotten on arrival and had to be destroyed. This shipment was evaluated at $63,900.
When we read the report of the Auditor General, we find many things and discover that some expenditures have been excessive. Here is an example of an expenditure which was unauthorized or not supported by vouchers or attestations:
(Mr. Clark.]
In 1975, the Canadian International Development Agency made a nugatory payment of $35,000 in respect of a claim made on termination of a transportation contract. This payment was made without the required approval of the Governor in Council.
Net losses attributable to fraud, default, or mistake of public employees totalled $217,131 in 1975-76 as reported in Section 12 of Volume I of the 1975-76 Public Accounts. Also, as a result of a mistake on a cheque requisition by the Department of National Revenue, a loss of $13,000 was incurred on the exchange of foreign currency.
At page 28 of the Conspectus of the report of the Auditor General, we find this:
My 1973 Report referred to deletion from the accounts of Canada of income tax revenue that could not be collected because the taxpayers were no longer resident in Canada. In 1976, such deletions amounted to $850,000 owed by 161 taxpayers. The Departments of Justice, National Revenue, and Finance are considering the question of confidentiality with respect to possible publication, as a deterrent measure, of the names of taxpayers whose accounts are written off.
We often find that the employees of the Department of National Revenue practically persecute small earners who do not have the financial means to pay their dues on time.
Quite often, they will go as far as garnisheeing the wages, without taking into account the needs of a family which, on top of its immediate needs, has to pay some bills regularly because of installments or other similar debts. Quite often, the employee is laid off on such an occasion because his employer does not want to be involved in the garnisheeing. Consequently, the worker is "overpenalized" in that sense.
Here are other irregularities relating to the wheat inventory reduction and grassland incentive payments. The aim of the wheat inventory reduction program, which was administered by the Department of Agriculture, was to take out of production up to 22 million acres of land in order to reduce the stock of surplus wheat. Under this program, farmers were eligible for a payment of $6 for each acre of cultivated land taken out of wheat in 1970 and summer-fallowed or planted to perennial forage. A further $4 per acre was payable with respect to land seeded to forage in 1970 and still in forage on July 15, 1971. Interim payments of $3 per acre were made on receipt of the applications and the balance of $3 per acre was paid following verification of the applications by reference to field inspection reports and aerial photographs. This method of payment resulted in some payments being in excess of the amount eventually determined as owing to the farmer, and at March 31, 1972, overpayments totalling $365,000 remained uncollected. This amount had been reduced to $288,000 by December 1, 1972.
I thought it was appropriate to quote that extract from the Report of the Auditor General for the financial year ending the March 31, 1972, first because it is not the first time that we hear about excessive spending and because, as I said earlier, I felt that it was appropriate to point out that problem to demonstrate two things: administrative errors about the payments relating to the reduction of the production of wheat, and the same thing happened in 1976 because of the method used to reduce the milk quotas. Instead of being compensated for over-production, milk producers are penalized because of their surpluses and, consequently, a high percentage of them are in a particularly dramatic situation.
December 1, 1976

By using means to eliminate excessive spending, I think it would have been possible to find a formula to compensate the milk producers who are at grips with the complicated problems we know.
The summary of the 1973 report of the Auditor General points out a host of administrative errors. I shall limit my comments to a few items only to demonstrate that it is not the first time the Auditor General brings the situation to the attention of the government. Here is a quotation from the summary of the 1973 report: Bad planification concerning the installation of computer systems. Almost $70,000 were spent for consultant and computer services without any apparent benefit for the Canada Council. Another point concerning offices rented unnecessarily by the Canadian Transport Commission: from November 1, 1968 to March 31, 1972, rental costs amounted to $1,898,000, including costs for offices that were not necessary in the opinion of the Auditor General.
It is obvious that if ordinary citizens realized those facts, they would feel a frustration that could lead them to revolt. It is fortunate for the government that our workers are not very interested in politics and not very aware of public issues.
I find that situation very sad as I have been myself a manual worker, I have been close to those who work hard for their living and I share their distress, the difficulties of those who are handicapped in front of a bureaucracy designed by people who do not care about the less privileged. You are not interested in high philosophy or you do not keep abreast with political and social realities when you are tired out or exhausted by physical and psychological burdens.
A great man once said: You can fool some people all the time, you can fool all the people sometime, but you can't fool all the people all the time. The truth in that quote became more than evident during a recent election somewhere in Canada. The government say they want a just society for every Canadian, but in my view this is still only a pious wish. Let them open their eyes to the have nots in our society, let them hear their grievances, and above all let them take heed.
A number of ancient cities were once prosperous and progressing as far as production and standards of living were concerned. Then suddenly something happened, and we wonder what. There must have been something, although we cannot pinpoint it. We then go on to wonder whether ours will be the same fate. We must go back through history, and remember what happened to the Turkish, the Roman, the Greek and the Moslem empires. Today the sun is setting on the British empire. What happened? What will become of us?
I believe that we ourselves are the makers of our doom. Our monetary system is self destroying. Our society is going through revolutions. Heavy burdens are laid on legislative parties, and taxes are crushingly high. The people themselves are divided. We have high costs of living and average revenues. We have a segregation between the poor and the rich, we have high production costs, we have disorder and chaos in our education system. This and many other factors lead me to the
Auditor General
conclusion that we are in a precarious position. Canadians today are concerned, they live with the fear that our democratic system will collapse, and the monetary system will crumble. We live in fear. It is time to reassess ourselves, to see what our position is in the world, to try and do something without delay.
I do not believe that the solution to the situation we are now discussing lies in the establishment of a commission. I remember in 1969 I had the following question standing in my name of the order paper:
How many study or investigating boards and commissions were appointed by the Canadian Government since 1950?
The answer was:
1. Fifty royal commissions of inquiry and three task forces.
And according to the list I have in front of me, I realize very well that the Glassco royal commission on government organization has cost $2,791,915 and that we are again faced with a similar situation. Therefore, I do not think that a commission of inquiry would solve our problem. More than 50 such commissions have cost over $1 million and as we can plainly see, the results have not been as expected.
Therefore I do not think that the government's decision to appoint a commission of inquiry would solve our problem. Let us accept the Auditor General's suggestions. He has the authority to make enquiries, to check the government's accounts and considering that we have chosen him for that posting he is certainly a trustworthy man. Having conferred with his colleagues, he suggests a way of so doing and we must not forget that the various auditors nominated to that position over the years have also made suggestions. I believe it is time that we accept that of the Auditor General.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE SERIOUSLY RECOMMENDATIONS OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in the debate on the opposition motion put forward by the leader of the New Democratic Party, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent). This is a subject which is very much in the national interest and it is to the hon. member's credit that he should have placed it before parliament at a time when certain supporters of his own party, particularly in provincial areas-I am thinking of British Columbia-might not be so anxious to talk about controls in the area of public expenditure. Notwithstanding these considerations, he has brought forward a motion on a subject in which the people of Canada are very interested, and I am pleased to participate in the debate. The leader of the New Democratic Party drew attention this afternoon to three specific matters. I should like to discuss each of them individually, but before doing so I should like to take a few minutes in which to review the background against which the debate has been proceeding-the entire subject of the Auditor General's report, government expenditure, financial control, or the lack of it, and so on.
It is important to understand some of the things that have been done in this House in the last few years on the government's initiative. The appointment of the present Auditor General was a very important step. In Mr. Macdonell we have

December 1, 1976
Auditor General
a man who I would describe as altogether different from the old style of accountant. We have a man who is professionally experienced as a qualified consultant, and in keeping with that kind of professional approach three important examinations have been initiated, with the co-operation of the government, since his appointment. First there was the study undertaken by the independent review committee. That committee, I believe, consisted entirely of professional people from outside. They came up with a very substantial report recommending significant changes in the responsibilities and functions of the office of Auditor General.
The government has acted on this report: we have before us in this session of parliament a new Auditor General's Act. It is my understanding that this is the first time the Canadian parliament has been given an Auditor General's Act. It is also my understanding that in the past the Auditor General has carried on his function under terms of reference that are found, I believe, in the Financial Administration Act. We are now going to have a completely new Auditor General's Act, the purpose of which will be to ensure that Auditors General in future in this country will have the kinds of responsibilities and authorities that the most modern professional opinion feels they should have in order adequately to report on the affairs, the expenditures and the revenues of government. I think that is a very important step. The government has not only indicated that it intends to adopt the recommendations, but it has placed before the House of Commons an act which I understand incorporates just about all the recommendations of the independent review committee. That is point number one.
Point number two, Mr. Speaker, is that another important study was undertaken, I believe in discussion with the Auditor General but more on the government's initiative, which was a review of the public accounts of Canada. That was a very comprehensive study. Those of us serving on the public accounts committee-I see some members sitting opposite who participated in the debate-will appreciate the size of the report alone which emanated from this particular examination. It was a very detailed review of how the government was doing its basic bookkeeping, its accounting of revenues and expenditures, its monthly financial reporting, the kind of report that is issued within departments and which is sent to central agencies and people outside.
There are some very substantial recommendations for change in that report, Mr. Speaker. I believe there were some 41 recommendations. We in the public accounts committee last year, a committee, I might add, contrary to what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) said earlier, which is an extremely effective committee in the House of Commons-

It is a committee of which I am proud at the present time to hold the position of vice-chairman. It is a committee that has been noted in the past for its impartial approach to the problems before it. I can only hope, and I am

sure it will be the case, that the committee will continue to act in an impartial manner. All members of parliament are interested in ensuring that the kinds of matters that come before the public accounts committee are handled in an efficient and effective way.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE SERIOUSLY RECOMMENDATIONS OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
I hear the comment from across the way that nobody listens. That is completely incorrect. The report of the public accounts of Canada came before us last year. We asked the President of the Treasury Board to make the clear statement, which he did indeed make, that all those recommendations would be implemented. It is such a detailed and voluminous report that the recommendations will take three or four years to get into the system. The Auditor General has said that he will comment annually on each recommendation that has been implemented or has not been been implemented, and he will report back in this way to the public accounts committee.
As for responsibility of government, the Leader of the Opposition commented earlier that this government is not responsible to parliament. How in the world can we be more responsible, Mr. Speaker, than the kinds of things that went on in connection with the review of these reports in our public accounts committee? In the second report there were 41 specific recommendations, all of which were important and are on their way to working themselves into the system.
Thirdly, Mr. Speaker, we had the financial management and control study, which was really an initiative of the Auditor General, which had the full support of the government. Out of that we heard the former President of the Treasury Board, the present Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien), tell us in the House a few minutes ago that 32 of the 34 recommendations in the report either have been implemented or are in the process of being implemented. If, Mr. Speaker, you add up 41 out of 41, and 32 out of 34, you get a very high and significant percentage of recommendations that are indeed being acted upon by the government at the present time. If that is what the opposition calls irresponsibility and lack of concern for the public and parliament, then I am afraid, like so many other arguments they put forward, I fail to understand the rationale.

speechtext: You cannot say that with a straight face.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO TAKE SERIOUSLY RECOMMENDATIONS OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
I thought it was important, Mr. Speaker, to put on the record the background of those three studies, and I should now like to deal specifically with the points raised by the leader of the New Democratic Party in his motion. The first part of his motion reads:
-to take steps to ensure that the annual financial reports of all Crown corporations are referred to the appropriate committees of the House of Commons-
In effect, Mr. Speaker, this happens now to some extent when individual agencies or Crown corporations come before the government for a review of their estimates or supplementary estimates. I am the first to say that it is probably
December 1, 1976

inadequate. We do not have very much time in our committee meetings to delve into the annual report of the corporation. Very often members on either side have other types of general questions that they want to address to the heads of corporations or agencies who may be before the committee at the time. Yet the annual reports are there and they are normally part of the material given to committee members. It is up to us as individual members of parliament, if we have questions to raise, to take the opportunity to raise those questions. I think we have to look at ourselves, at the kind of performance we give and the way in which we undertake our responsibilities in committees.
I am not entirely speaking against the motion of the leader of the New Democratic Party, Mr. Speaker, but my concern is that there are so many Crown corporations or agencies of various categories and types. I understand they fall under seven or eight categories. There is a departmental corporation category, of which something like the National Research Council is an example-one of the many. There are agency corporations, of which the National Capital Commission is an example. There are proprietary corporations, of which the CNR and CBC are examples. There are unclassified corporations, of which the Bank of Canada or the Canadian Wheat Board are examples. Then there is a category known as "other corporations", and I have no idea what is in that category.
If we were to insist that each one of these annual reports was to come before the appropriate committee of this House for detailed consideration by the committee, my concern is that the work of the committee would be concentrated on that particular matter for so much of its time-indeed, on those matters because more than one Crown corporation could be reporting to the same standing committee-that it would be very difficult for the committee to deal with other work that is before it, including new legislation, all of which is referred to the committee after second reading in the House. So I would be interested in hearing more about this. I just do not know how it could be done physically within the system.
I disagree completely with the Leader of the Opposition. He feels that committes are-I forget his terminology, but he used the term "fraudulent". I think he was referring to the manner in which they are established. I have yet, in my 2'A years in this House, to participate in a committee where I have not felt completely free to ask any question that might come into my head regarding the operations of a particular department, Crown corporation or agency. I think the committee system is excellent. However, it can always be improved. My understanding is that it is a big improvement now over what it was in the days when for a short period in Canadian history the government was administered by people on the other side.
Maybe committees do not have clout, although I do not agree with that entirely. Recommendations can be made in committee for legislative changes and then come into the House. Certainly, the public accounts committee has had a lot of clout. In fact, the Auditor General has told us that without our committee he can go nowhere. He depends on our committee to support him in the kind of work he undertakes. I think
Auditor General
he would be the first to say that if it were not for the support and back-up of the public accounts committee, then the kinds of reports that he has presented this year and last year would not have been nearly as effective. The mere fact that he quoted in his report comments by myself and other committee members indicates that he felt they were important enough to back up his work. In my view, the committee system is terribly important, so important that I am not sure we can handle the kind of request the leader of the NDP is proposing in the suggestion that all reports of agencies and Crown corporations come before us.
The next point the leader of the NDP has contained in his motion is:
(b)	to provide the Standing Committee on Public Accounts with adequate staff so that it can do its job thoroughly-
I agree completely. I think this is the first committee with which I have had experience in this House that has had a permanent researcher assigned to it since I have been associated with the committee. Just yesterday the chairman of the public accounts committee-and, I might say, without discussing this with the steering committee first, and I think we will forgive him in this instance because it was quite a positive move that he made-did approach the research branch of the library and requested that an additional person be allocated to the research back-up for that committee. I understand we now have a young lawyer who has been seconded from the library to the committee. It is my belief the committee will be free at any time, if we need additional research back-up, to make that request, and I do not envisage it being turned down. I have no trouble in agreeing completely with that recommendation of the leader of the NDP. The only thing I would say is that I think basically, his request is probably being implemented, and if it is not adequately, then I think it is up to those of us in the public accounts committee to make sure we get the kind of research back-up that we want. The third part of his motion is as follows:
(c)	to appoint immediately a comptroller general as recommended in the Auditor General's report for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1976.
That is the one that gets a little bit dicey. As a former financial officer in industry and an active member of the public accounts committee and a member of the committee on finance, it is my personal feeling that any large organization does need a chief financial officer. I think those of us in the public accounts committee have felt this all along. The Auditor General obviously had a little difficulty with this matter. In his 1975 report he hinted at it, but he really only came out firmly on the thing when we pinned him down, if I might use that phraseology, in the public accounts committee last spring when we said, "Now look Mr. Macdonell, are you, or are you not, recommending a chief financial officer position?" When he was pinned down in that way he said, "Yes, indeed, that is what I am recommending".
The reason I mention that is simply that in his own mind, and I am sure in the mind of his senior people, he had to

December 1, 1976
Auditor General
wrestle with this one himself for a good deal of time before he was prepared to stand four-square behind it. The reasons for that are very evident to anybody who has had any involvement in large business where that kind of position has not been invoked before. The only way in which a position such as that can become effective is if it is accepted by his colleagues in the organization right across the board. That is terribly important, and it is not something that can just happen merely by saying, "There is the position of chief financial officer, and there is the body we put into that position. Good luck, and we hope it all works out".
I have no difficulty in realizing that it is quite appropriate for those who are ultimately responsible for the operation of government, which is the government in power, to sit back and look at this kind of recommendation and say that it is a recommendation over which the Auditor General himself puzzled for a very considerable time before making it, and we had better take a very close look at this to see how it is going to work into the system. The appointment of a royal commission seems to me, by its very terms, to support itself whether or not the position of a chief financial officer is part of the package.
We must all realize that it is 17 years or so since the appointment of the Glassco commission, which was the first honest look at the manner in which government operations were carried out. The level of expenditures in the country were then some $6 billion. If Mr. Glassco himself were alive today, I am sure he would be the first to say that in order to make that kind of recommendation effective over the long term, we will have to look at the situation periodically down the road. I suggest that is basically what the royal commission, which will probably become known as the Lambert commission, is going to do, and it will be doing so at a time when the level of expenditures is up to $40 billion of $42 billion, more than six times what it was before.
It will be doing this at a time when growth in the civil service has expanded tremendously and when the whole system is far more complicated than ever before. To suggest it is wrong at this time to have a royal commission look into the over-all financial operations of the government, I suggest, is really to take a position that basically suggests this was done 20 years ago so we should not worry. That simply is not good enough in this day and age, because things are changing too dramatically.
In concluding my remarks on the royal commission, I should like to say that in my view the kind of recommendations that can come out of such a commission, which from a central point I do not think will be dealing with this matter of a chief financial officer, could help guide us or the government in deciding whether, as a result of the Glassco commission, the strings of control were cut a little too loose, with over-all decentralization to the point where things are floating around a little bit, and with the endeavour to keep them under sort of tight control disappearing altogether.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to enter this debate in support of the motion placed before the House by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent). I was very impressed by the contribution of the Leader of Her Majesty's Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) and by his frank assessment and evaluation of this government in pointing out that the elements of cynicism, arrogance and incompetence have become the hallmarks of this administration. I am sure hon. members enjoyed the contribution of that little country boy lawyer from Quebec, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien). Even though he missed the significance of this motion, he provided us with an afternoon of fun and merriment. I guess he was out looking for bigger game than a comptroller general. In all seriousness, I must say I am appalled by the way the minister tried to diffuse the urgency of this problem. I think he was less than frank with this House in dealing with the importance and the reality of the situation before us as referred to in this motion.
Today I want primarily to deal with the preamble to the motion that refers to the failure of the government to take seriously the recommendations that have been made year after year by the auditor general, not only the present one but his predecessor. It is certainly worthy of note that if we go back to 1973 we will find the former auditor general advanced some 34 recommendations in his report of that year which were dealt with by the public accounts committee and which have not yet been implemented. We all know that this government was at loggerheads with the former auditor general. While the government did not clip his wings completely, it certainly attempted to stifle his effectiveness and therefore affected his ability to discharge his mandate to parliament and the people of Canada. Deliberate action was taken by this government to reduce his effectiveness. The government downgraded his staff and failed to provide him with adequate personnel and resources to do his job. There was a constant on-going conflict between him and the president of the Treasury Board, and indeed the Prime Minister.
Despite the comment made by the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Martin), there was a new Auditor General's Act presented to this House in 1970 which would have had the effect of curtailing his powers. We all know what happened at that time. The public looked on this act with such indignation concerning the proposals in respect of the Auditor General that the government saw fit to withdraw that legislation. I am surprised that the hon. member for Scarborough West did not realize this. We had a proposed act in 1970. There was another occasion in 1973 when the public accounts committee presented a draft for a new Auditor General's Act which never saw the light of day.
This is, in effect, the third attempt. The fact remains that in spite of the ongoing feud between the government and the former auditor general, he did carry out a very effective job on
December 1, 1976

behalf of the people of Canada. I want to cite some of the recommendations which remained on the table when he left office in 1973. Some of them date back to 1964. For example, we have recommendation No. 16 at page 138 of the 1973 auditor general's report. It deals with loans and advances representing grants to Crown corporations.
Just to cite the situation briefly, the committee again criticized the practice of treating amounts paid by Crown corporations which did not have the means to pay them. That is also contained in the 1976 auditor general's report. We could go on to recommendation No. 23 at page 141 in respect of parliamentary control of expenditures. This goes back to the thirteenth report of the public accounts committee in 1966-67. Recommendation No. 29 has to do with increasing accommodation rental costs. This is at page 143. In the report for 1976 we have a reference to wasteful accommodation. The fact of the matter is that these recommendations were outstanding in 1973, are still outstanding in 1976, and no action has been taken.
Let us put this in perspective. There have been progress reports which I do not have the time to review in detail. However, if one looks at them one will detect that they involve nothing more than delaying tactics, with the suggestion that the matter is under review, that it is being studied or considered. The very vague wording suggests that little or no action is being taken in most of these cases. The hon. member for Scarborough West indicated that 32 recommendations were endorsed and supported by the government. He said that is great, that the government agrees. But what has been done? On page 37 of this year's auditor general's report we have a very clear indication of just how much progress has been made toward implementing these recommendations. So far as I am concerned, there is a great deal of difference between the acceptance of recommendations and their implementation. They may have been accepted, but certainly they have not been implemented to any great extent. The Auditor General says:
-six recommendations where positive action is clearly indicated but without any indication of its form or timing.
- 16 recommendations where there appears to be agreement, but no clear indication of planned corrective action; and
-12 recommendations where some disagreement has already been expressed and there is no indication of alternative corrective action.
That is the fact of the matter. That is what has happened to the 34 recommendations. Only six of the 34 have been acted on, and only to a very limited degree. That is where we stand today, and that is what the debate is all about. This simply means that the government has blatantly disregarded the recommendations of the Auditor General. If the government does not intend to implement them, this means it is disregarding them and I say that is a cavalier attitude.

I am glad I flushed out the hon. member, because I will deal with that progress report which was presented to the House. I will show the House what a stupid, hilarious document it is, because when one analyses it one will find in absolute terms that this government is engaged in a game of perpetuating bureaucratic jargon rather than implementing the important recommendations in this area. I say it is a blatant disregard of the office of the Auditor General. I say it is disregard for parliament and the public accounts committee because, quite frankly, the public accounts committee unanimously endorsed those 34 recommendations. There is no question about that.
We hear so much about the role of parliament and the concern over the appointment of a comptroller general, because this might affect the effectiveness of parliament. Well, these birds certainly never regarded the recommendations of a parliamentary committee with any great degree of importance, certainly not the degree of importance they so richly deserve. This also means that the government has failed parliament and the people of Canada by not acting responsibly in administering public funds.
I mentioned the financial management and control study which arises out of the very comprehensive and most objective professional analysis and examination of the government's financial management and control mechanisms. We were presented with some 34 very sound recommendations. These were not the recommendations of the Auditor General alone: there were some 150,000 professional man-hours involved in putting together the recommendations. They were the result of a very detailed and comprehensive study. I said earlier that they were endorsed by the public accounts committee. I might say that the government agreed with some 22, extended qualified agreement to 10, and disagreed with 2.
The former president of the Treasury Board announced the creation of a new branch within the Treasury Board responsible for financial administration, headed by a person with deputy secretary status who would have the status of an assistant deputy minister in other departments. This, in the eyes of the Auditor General-and I must say I agree-is ineffective since the deputy secretary is placed in the position of assessing and analysing the work of his peers. The position demands more status and more clout. The government, by agreeing to the 22 recommendations, has admitted that the control systems are not satisfactory, that they are significantly below acceptable standards, but it has failed to respond by taking the necessary corrective action to clean up this mess. It has failed to establish a system which would be considered acceptable to those acquainted with the accounting profession in this country.

December 1, 1976
Auditor General
While the establishment of the financial administration branch may be a step in the right direction, the branch does not have adequate resources, and I will refer to that in more detail in a little while. In my view this is a very shallow response to a very urgent problem. It is tantamount to using an aspirin to cure a severe case of pneumonia. What is more significant-and this is what appears so unreasonable on the part of the government and the elitists in the bureaucracy-is that these recommendations from the management and control branch are essentially a follow-up from the Glassco commission's recommendations. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce spoke at great length about the fact that the recommendations of the Glassco commission have been incorporated. That is not really so, because we have heard evidence before the Standing Committee on Public Accounts time after time that although these recommendations certainly flow from the report of the Glassco commission, many of them have not been properly implemented.
Let me quote from the proceedings of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts, issue No. 45, page 66. Mr. Dale Harris of the Auditor General's office stated the following:
-virtually all of the observations and recommendations in our report were provided for, to a greater or lesser extent, by the Glassco commission in 1962. Our recommendations are consistent with Glassco in that they vary only in emphasis and degree of detail. The evidence indicates that those responsible chose not to emphasize or implement most of the control-oriented recommendations.
I should also like to quote Mr. Lafferty as recorded at page 13 of the committee's proceedings, issue No. 50, as follows:
It is also our view that until departments introduce effective systems of budgetary control, there is no basis for determining whether or not funds are being spent for the purposes, in terms of activities, for which they were provided.
I will go on to quote the Auditor General as recorded at page 7 of issue No. 51 of the committee's proceedings. He said:
-the resources of the Treasury Board are far too low, not in quality, but certainly in numbers, to cope with such a major responsibility as financial management control.
These are matters to which parliament and the Auditor General are addressing themselves, and these are the salient features of this problem. The progress report which was tabled by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) some ten days ago refers to the role of the new financial administration branch. He sees it as an over-all panacea and a way of resolving the bulk of the problems brought to light by the Auditor General. Whenever the minister rises in the House to answer a question from a member of the opposition, he waves this progress report and orders us to read it. I must say that I have read it over and over again and I am appalled at the fact that the President of the Treasury Board would rely on this document to fend off the criticisms that have been levelled against him and his government.
I want to deal with that progress report to demonstrate the extent to which the government expects to correct everything in the area of government operations, from preparing a response to the Auditor General's report to formulating a

policy for the use and control of departmental credit cards. I do not see how the minister can be serious in using this report to answer the serious questions that have been posed by members of the opposition. Surely the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce cannot hang his hat on this report in defending his government.
Let us look at the responsibilities assigned to this branch. They are all-encompassing. It is a rather innovative superstructure which undertakes to perform many duties but does very little in the way of establishing real control and management of public funds. I should like to point out some of the duties spelled out here that have been assigned to the financial administration branch, and then I want to deal with the resources that have been given to this branch to point out the sheer folly of this particular mechanism. The following is a quotation from the progress report tabled by the President of the Treasury Board some ten days ago:
-the responsibilities of the financial administration branch . . . include:
(a)	the development and evaluation of financial administration policies;
(b)	the development and evaluation of internal audit policies and standards;
(c)	the formulation and maintenance of the accounting principles and standards that are used in the accounts of Canada and in the preparation of the public accounts;
(d)	the provision of advice on the content of the estimates for the purposes of budgetary and financial control and for consistency and continuity with the content of the Canada Gazette series and the public accounts of Canada;
(e)	the development and evaluation of principles and guidelines for financial systems;
(f)	the provision of a central advisory service to departments and agencies concerning accounting and auditing policies and principles, together with the provision of uniform interpretations of financial administration legislation, policies and guidelines;
(g)	the development and maintenance, in conjunction with the Public Service Commission, of professional development programs for financial officers and auditors in the federal public service;
(h)	the co-ordination and preparation of the government's response to the Auditor General's annual report and the presentation of this response to the public accounts committee.
The progress report goes on to refer to the following:
The ongoing, day to day business of the branch includes processing, or advising on, submissions made to the Treasury Board, providing advice to departments and agencies on all financial administrative matters-a function which is growing significantly-and conducting more detailed evaluations of departmental application and implementation of the Treasury Board's financial administration policies.
